desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. A transaction is one purchase of a single share followed by a sale on a strictly later day; you can hold at most one share at a time, so the next purchase may happen on the day of the previous sale but not earlier.

Return the smallest number of transactions with which the total profit can reach at least target, or -1 if even unlimited transactions cannot reach it.

Example: prices = [1,5,2,6,3,7]. One transaction earns at most 6, two at most 9 and three at most 12. For target = 9 the answer is 2; for target = 13 it is -1.
hints: Let F(k) be the maximum profit with at most k transactions. F never decreases with k, so you are looking for the first k with F(k) ≥ target. Doing the k-transaction DP for every k is too slow for n = 4000.
F(k) is concave: each extra transaction adds no more than the one before it. So F(k) is the sum of the k largest 'marginal gains' of some fixed list.

Walk the prices keeping a stack of rising segments (valley, peak). When a new segment starts lower or ends higher than earlier ones, merge them and record the profit that is given up or gained. Sort all recorded profits in descending order and take prefix sums until the target is reached.
editorial: Decompose the price curve into maximal rising runs (valley to peak). Optimal solutions with k transactions are built from these runs: with fewer transactions than runs you must either drop the least valuable run or merge two neighbouring runs, and every such step costs as little as possible. This produces a fixed multiset of 'marginal gains' g1 ≥ g2 ≥ ... and F(k) = g1 + ... + gk.

The stack procedure builds exactly that multiset. Keep a stack of (valley, peak) pairs. For each new run (v, p): while the top pair has a higher valley than v, pop it and record its own profit (it is a finished, independent run); then while the top pair has a lower peak than p, merge: pop it, record peak_of_popped - v and extend the new run to start at the popped valley. Push the run. At the end pop everything and record each pair's profit.

Sort the recorded gains in descending order and accumulate until the sum reaches the target; the number of gains used is the answer, and -1 if their total is below the target. The scan is O(n) and the sort O(n log n). A binary search on k with the O(nk) DP is far too slow; this concavity is the key insight.
